notesStmt.note: Based on Whitman's note, this manuscript dates from sometime in November or December 1890.

This is a proof slip for a cluster of poems that was seemingly never published in this configuration or under this title, although the poems were all published, in some form, in Good-Bye My Fancy (1891). The poems included are: "Ancient Songs Reciting" (later retitled "Old Chants"), "Grand is the seen," "Death dogs my steps" (published as part of "L. of G.'s Purport"), and "For us two, reader dear." Another extant proof slip, titled "Old Age Recitatives," contains some although not all of the same poems. Whitman's note on an earlier version of that cluster state that he submitted it to Arena magainze in November 1890 but that it was rejected. The present proof slip is thus seeminglty a re-worked version of this earlier cluster.

lg.l: An ancient song,‸Ancient songs reciting, ending,
Once gazing toward thee, Mother of All,
Musing, seeking themes fitted for thee,
Accept for me, thou saidst, the‸those elder ballads,
And name for me before thou goest each ancient poet.
(Of many debts incalculable,
Haply our New World's chiefest debt is to old poems.
Ever so far back, preluding thee, America,
Old chants, Egyptian priests, and those of Ethiopia,
The Hindu epics, the Grecian, Chinese, Persian,

The Biblic books and prophets, and deep idylls of the Naza-
reneNazarene
,
The Iliad, Odyssey, plots, doings, wanderings of Eneas,
Hesiod, Eschylus, Sophocles, Merlin, Arthur
The Cid, Roland at Roncesvalles, the Nibelungen,
The troubadours, minstrels, minnesingers, skalds
Chaucer, Dante, flocks of singing birds,

The Border Minstrelsy, the bye-gone ballads, feudal tales,
essays, plays,
Shakespere, Schiller, Walter Scott, Tennyson
As some vast wondrous wierd dream-presences,
The great shadowy groups gathering around,
Darting their mighty masterful eyes forward at thee,

Thou! with as now thy bending neck and head, with courte-
ouscourteous
hand and word, ascending,

Thou! pausing a moment, drooping thine eyes upon them,
blent with their music,
Well pleased, accepting all, curiously prepared for by them,
Thy enterest at thy entrance porch.

Grand is the seen, the light, to me—grand are the sky and
stars,
Grand is the earth, and grand are lasting time and space,
And grand their laws, so multiform, puzzling, evolutionary;

But grander far the unseen soul of me, comprehending, en-
dowingendowing
all those.,

Lighting the light, the sky and stars, delving the earth, sailing
the sea,
More evolutionary, vast, puzzling, O my soul!
More multiform far—more lasting thou than they.
I sing of life, yet mind me well of death:

To-day shadowy Death dogs my steps, and has for years—my
seated shape,
Draws sometimes closer to me, as face to face.
Simple, spontaneous, curious, two souls interchanging,
With the original testimony for us continued on to the last.
